titulo: Phrasal Verbs, Collocation and Register Shift
subtitulo: Dropping register on purpose inside a formal text
descripcion: At C2 the register ladder from look into to investigate to conduct an inquiry into extends further: the writer can shift register mid-text on purpose, dropping into the informal end for rhetorical effect within an otherwise formal piece, and knows exactly how far that shift can go before it breaks the whole register.

filas: reads as a slip, not a choice
can read as flat if never varied

ejemplos.texto: The committee conducted a thorough review — and, frankly, found a mess.
It's a great pub, though I should note it lacks any semblance of a wine list.
The report found nothing; in plainer terms, the whole exercise was wasted.

notas: A single deliberate register shift, well placed, reads as control and personality; two or more in the same short text reads as inconsistency.
The shift works best right after a formal or technical passage, where the contrast is sharpest.
In plainer terms and frankly are useful, controlled bridges from formal to informal register.

contraste.es: Formal Spanish tolerates a deliberate change of register within one text less than contemporary English, where a single well-placed informal turn counts as style rather than carelessness. Spanish speakers at C2 therefore tend to avoid register shifts altogether and lose a rhetorical tool professional English expects.
contraste.de: Separable verbs give German speakers a structural feel for phrasal verbs, so the forms themselves are easy. What is less familiar is the deliberate drop into informal register within a formal text, which German professional writing generally avoids, so German speakers keep the whole piece at the Latinate end.
contraste.it: Because Latinate English verbs are transparent to Italian speakers (investigate – investigare), the formal end of the register ladder feels safest. The deliberate drop into a phrasal verb for rhetorical effect is less familiar, as formal Italian tends to stay at one register throughout a text.
contraste.fr: Latinate English verbs are transparent to French speakers (investigate – enquêter, investiguer), and formal French writing keeps a stable, carefully policed register. French speakers therefore stay at the formal end and rarely risk a deliberate informal turn in English.
contraste.pt: Latinate English verbs are transparent to Portuguese speakers (investigate – investigar), so the formal end of the ladder feels safest. The deliberate informal turn within a formal text is less common in Portuguese professional writing and has to be practised as a conscious stylistic choice.

errores: Shifting register more than once in a short text, which breaks consistency instead of adding effect.
Placing the informal shift somewhere it isn't set up by a preceding formal passage.
Avoiding any register shift at all, which reads as flat in a genre that expects some variation.

es: Defaulting to the Latinate cognate (*commence*, *terminate*, *obtain*) because it matches Spanish, which makes neutral prose sound stiff.
de: Calquing German separable verbs as phrasal verbs: *make on the light* from *das Licht anmachen* instead of *turn on the light*.
it: Defaulting to the Latinate cognate (*commence*, *terminate*, *obtain*) because it matches Italian, which makes neutral prose sound stiff.
fr: Defaulting to the Latinate cognate (*commence*, *terminate*, *obtain*) because it matches French, which makes neutral prose sound stiff.
pt: Defaulting to the Latinate cognate (*commence*, *terminate*, *obtain*) because it matches Portuguese, which makes neutral prose sound stiff.

mision.consigna: Write a formal letter to an authority about a process that has left you in limbo — with one deliberate drop into plain speech.
requisitos: one controlled drop into the informal end for rhetorical effect
one *which is a polite way of saying…*
use *red tape*, *to be in limbo* and *to navigate the system*

microtareas.texto: Write the ladder for *get the runaround*: three rungs from phrasal to formal.
Draft the sentence where the register drops. Is it a punch or a slip?
Record 2 minutes describing *a Kafkaesque process* you went through.

autochequeo: Is there at most one deliberate register shift in a short text?
Is the shift set up by the surrounding register, not jarring?
Does the shift add effect rather than read as an accident?
Would an expert reader sense authorial control here?
Does the text also have a genre-appropriate baseline register, not just the shift?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on deliberate register shifts. Check that there's at most one, and that it's set up by the surrounding text rather than jarring. Do not rewrite the text.
